insights.headline: He claims fairness and non-blame ("I want to be fair on that") while his own retirement and departures show he preempts being judged or chosen against.
insights.explanation: In E3 he insists Deb "never said the word" and takes pains to frame the divorce as mutual and fair. Yet in E5 he takes the buyout before the layoff list comes out specifically so he won't "find out" if he was on it — the same instinct to leave before being told something unwanted, rather than to stay and learn the outcome. The stated self-image is someone who waits for the facts and stays fair; the lived pattern is someone who exits pre-emptively to control the narrative of his own departure.
insights.narrator_frame: "She didn't ask me to go. I want to be fair on that."

insights.would_predict: Mindset and limiting beliefs: facing an upcoming evaluation or decision about him (a medical diagnosis, a will, a performance review), he will act to resolve or exit the uncertainty himself rather than wait for the outcome to be delivered.

insights.headline: Every experience ends with a small, deliberately minimizing sign-off that undercuts what he just described.
insights.explanation: "Anyway. That's the shop" (E1); "Anyway that's the twelfth" (E2); "Anyway. Duke lived till oh-nine" (E3); "Anyway that's the — that's it, that's the story. Not much of one" (E5). The pattern spans four of five experiences and always deflates the preceding content immediately after he's shown unusual specificity or feeling, suggesting a reflexive move to close down significance right after it surfaces.
insights.narrator_frame: "Not much of one" (E5) — explicit self-deprecation about the value of his own account

evidence.quote: Anyway. That's the shop.
Anyway that's the — that's it, that's the story. Not much of one.

insights.falsifier: If he ends an account on the emotional or significant beat itself, without a deflecting closer, this form pattern weakens.
insights.would_predict: Personal growth: asked to reflect on an accomplishment (41 years worked, a marriage, raising a son), he will conclude with a minimizing phrase ("not much," "that's it") rather than an evaluative or proud statement.

insights.headline: Across five stories spanning a heart attack, a divorce, and a death, he never once names what he wanted for himself.
insights.explanation: He states what tasks needed doing (parts, trucks, furnaces, tools) and what others needed (Deb's furnace, Nick's rod, Devon's mics) in granular detail, but there is no instance across the corpus where he articulates a personal want or preference independent of a task — not about the divorce, not about retirement, not about the stent recovery, not even about the fishing rod's purpose beyond Nick's hockey colors. The corpus gives ample room for this (a whole account of quitting the second cardiac medication, a whole account of retiring) and it never surfaces.

evidence.quote: The other one made my legs hurt so I quit that, I didn't — I mean I meant to call about it.

insights.falsifier: If in any account he states a preference or want framed around himself ("I wanted X") rather than a task or another person, this absence claim fails.
insights.would_predict: Passions and interests: asked directly "what do you want to do now that you're retired," he will answer with a routine (Denny's, same wake time) rather than a goal or desire.

insights.headline: No story contains a moment where he receives help; every account shows him giving, fixing, or providing, never being on the receiving end.
insights.explanation: He drives himself to the hospital for a 90%-blocked artery (E4), fixes Deb's furnace and tires alone (E3), builds tools and toys for others (E2, E5), moves his own furniture with one coworker rather than a crew (E3) — but at no point does anyone fix, drive, build, or care for him, even in the moment of his own cardiac event, where a spouse's or partner's care would ordinarily appear. Given a heart attack, a divorce, and a retirement are exactly the events where being helped is common, this is a meaningful gap rather than an artifact of topic choice.

insights.falsifier: If any account describes someone else initiating care toward him that he accepts, this absence claim fails.
insights.would_predict: Friendships and community: he will not have a person he names as someone he calls first in a crisis; asked "who would you call," he will hesitate or name a task-based contact (a mechanic, a doctor) rather than a person.

insights.headline: The retirement account reveals that his entire style of care — quiet transfer of tools, minimized exits — is a closed system he learned from Walt and never revised.
insights.explanation: E1 alone shows a moving anecdote about receiving a mic in silence. Only with E5 present can we see it was not a singular memory but a template he actively re-enacted on Devon forty years later, down to the concealment of the gift's source and the flat closing line. This means the Walt story is not nostalgia but evidence of an operating procedure still running the day he left the workforce for good.

insights.would_predict: Leadership and collaboration: in any future mentoring relationship he enters, he will transfer knowledge or resources indirectly/anonymously rather than through direct praise or acknowledgment.

insights.headline: He names coworkers and their competence with more evaluative detail than he gives any family member.
insights.explanation: Rigo "couldn't hold a tenth to save his life" (E2), Devon has "good hands, terrible with a print" (E5), Timmy Pahl is named in a single functional mention (E3) — these are specific, opinionated character assessments. By contrast, Deb and Nick receive almost no adjectival description of their character anywhere in the corpus; Nick is described only by inherited trait ("his mother's way of going quiet") and Deb almost not at all except logistically.

insights.would_predict: Family and parenting: asked to describe Nick's strengths and weaknesses the way he describes a coworker's skill, he will default to biography (job, location, visit frequency) rather than character assessment.
